scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. However, I’ll break it down from **psychological, relational, and ethical perspectives** to help you reflect on whether your action was *reasonable* or *unnecessary* in this context. Here’s my analysis: --- ### **1. The Ethical Lens: Was It Right?** **Yes, it was ethically justified—but with nuance.** - **Respect for Your Brother**: You’re advocating for your half-brother’s well-being by protecting him from language that could be hurtful or stigmatizing (e.g., "baby mama" carries connotations of illegitimacy or shame, which may affect his identity later). This is a **moral responsibility** as a sibling. - **Your Own Emotional Boundaries**: You’re not asking your mom to *like* the girlfriend or treat her with warmth—just to **avoid demeaning language in front of you**. This is a **boundary-setting** action, not an attack on her feelings. Boundaries are healthy, even in difficult family dynamics. - **Avoiding Re-traumatization**: The term "baby mama" can dredge up painful memories of your parents’ divorce and the emotional fallout. By asking for neutral language, you’re **protecting your mental space**, which is valid. **Where it could be seen as "wrong":** - If your mom’s use of the term was **private** (only between her and her friends) and didn’t affect you or your brother, your intervention might feel like **overstepping**. However, since it was happening *in front of you*, it’s not unreasonable to address it. - If you’d **never** asked her to stop calling her by name at all (e.g., "she" instead of "baby mama"), it might feel like you’re asking for too much. But you didn’t—you just asked for **neutrality**, which is a lower bar. --- ### **2. The Relational Lens: Was It Wise?** **It was a calculated risk with potential payoffs.** - **Pros of Your Action:** - You **modeled respect** for your brother’s relationship with his mother. This could help him later when he’s older and might feel the sting of stigma. - You **set a precedent** for how you want to be treated in family conflicts (e.g., "I won’t tolerate disrespect, even if it’s ‘just words’"). - You **acknowledged your mom’s feelings** by apologizing for making her feel disrespected. This shows emotional intelligence. - **Cons/Risks:** - Your mom’s reaction suggests she **interprets the term as a label of her own worth**. If she feels "baby mama" is tied to her identity (e.g., "She’s not my wife, so she’s less than me"), then asking her to stop might feel like you’re **erasing her pain**. This is why she got defensive—she may have been projecting her own hurt onto the term. - If your mom is **stubborn or emotionally volatile**, she might see this as you "taking sides" with your dad’s girlfriend, even if that wasn’t your intent. This could strain your relationship further. **Key Question:** *Did your mom’s use of the term actually harm you or your brother?* If the answer is "yes" (e.g., it made you feel disrespected or triggered memories), then your action was **necessary**. If it was just a habit she didn’t realize was hurtful, then she might need **gentler guidance** (e.g., "Mom, I know you’re upset, but could we try calling her by her name when I’m around?"). --- ### **3. The Psychological Lens: Why Did Your Mom React So Strongly?** Her anger likely stems from: - **Guilt/Shame**: She may feel guilty for her role in the divorce and unconsciously lash out at the "intruder" (the girlfriend) to protect her own ego. - **Fear of Losing Control**: The term "baby mama" might feel like a **power dynamic**—she’s reclaiming agency by demeaning the girlfriend, even if it’s just in language. - **Projection**: She may associate the term with **how she felt when she found out about the affair** (betrayal, humiliation), so she’s not just calling the girlfriend—she’s calling *your dad’s infidelity*. **This doesn’t excuse her behavior, but it explains why she reacted so defensively.** It’s not about the term itself—it’s about **what it symbolizes to her**. --- ### **4. The "AITA" Verdict: <1> (With Caveats)** I’d rate this as a **1 (mildly justified, but could have been handled differently)** for these reasons: - **You had a valid reason** to ask (protecting your brother and your own feelings). - **You handled it with empathy** (you apologized and acknowledged her feelings). - **But:** You could have **framed it more collaboratively** to avoid triggering her defensiveness. For example: > *"Mom, I know you’re upset, and I get that this is hard for you. But when you call her ‘baby mama’ in front of me, it makes me feel like we’re rehashing old wounds. Could we try calling her by her name when I’m around? It would help me feel more comfortable with her."* This version: - **Validates her feelings** (reduces defensiveness). - **Shifts focus to your needs** (not attacking her). - **Offers a compromise** (she doesn’t have to like the girlfriend, just use neutral language). --- ### **5. What Now? Moving Forward** Since you’ve already addressed this, here’s how to **repair or maintain the relationship**: - **Reinforce boundaries gently**: If she slips up again, say: > *"I know you’re stressed, but I really need us to talk about her with respect when I’m around."* - **Redirect conversations**: If she starts badmouthing her, steer the topic elsewhere: > *"Mom, I’d rather talk about [neutral topic]. How’s [your job/grandkid’s school/etc.] going?"* - **Model the behavior you want**: If you’re civil with her, she may eventually follow suit. - **Accept her limits**: If she can’t change, **you can’t control that**. Focus on what *you* can control (your own reactions, your brother’s environment). --- ### **Final Thought: Was It Worth It?** **Yes, if:** - It made you feel **less triggered** or **more respected**. - It helped your brother **feel more included** in the family. - It **didn’t destroy your relationship with your mom** (which it didn’t, based on your description). **No, if:** - It **escalated tension** without any long-term benefit. - Your mom **still uses the term** and you’re now in an awkward dynamic. In this case, it seems like a **small win**—you stood up for what mattered to you without causing irreparable harm. That’s **adulting well**. --- ### **TL;DR:** You were **not "wrong"** for asking—it was a **reasonable boundary** for your emotional and familial well-being. However, **how you asked could have been softer** to avoid her defensiveness. The reaction was more about *her* unresolved feelings than the term itself. **You handled it maturely**, and that’s what matters most.
